title: Why You Should Never Give Choices Instead Of Consequences -of-consequences/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin sharply criticizes the trend of offering misbehaving students appealing alternatives (working on the rug, using an iPad, taking a break) instead of enforcing a warranted consequence. Using a hypothetical student, Jason, Linsin illustrates how negotiating choices in place of accountability temporarily stops disruption but sends a corrosive long-term message: that misbehavior can be bargained away, that the student is incapable of change, and that they are being defined by their misbehavior rather than held to a standard. He lists ten specific harms of this approach, including reinforcing entitlement, damaging trust with the rest of the class, and stripping students of dignity more effectively than yelling or sarcasm would. Linsin's alternative is unambiguous: follow the classroom management plan and give consequences, framing consistent accountability as an expression of belief in students' capability rather than punishment.
points: Offering misbehaving students appealing alternatives instead of consequences temporarily stops disruption but is argued to cause serious long-term harm.
The practice sends the message that misbehavior can be negotiated away, reinforcing entitlement and encouraging more frequent, more severe misbehavior over time.
It implicitly labels students as incapable of behavioral change, a label Linsin argues is devastating and self-fulfilling for difficult students.
Ten specific harms are enumerated, including damaged trust with the rest of the class, stripped dignity, and undermined teacher leadership and consistency.
The recommended alternative is straightforward: follow the classroom management plan and issue consequences, framed as an expression of belief in students' capability rather than punishment.
quotes: One of the more perplexing trends in classroom management is to give students choices instead of consequences.
The idea is to remove the source of his discontentment, to entice him with alternatives so that he will no longer engage in unwanted behavior.

When you appease difficult students by lowering academic or behavioral standards, you send an unmistakable message that they can complain, disrupt, and misbehave their way out of anything they deem unpleasant.

By giving in so readily, even voluntarily, you’re essentially telling them that you believe they’re incapable of changing their behavior. This is a form of labeling, and it is devastating to difficult students.

Letting students off the hook is akin to telling them they’re not good enough or worthy enough to be held to a higher standard, which strips away dignity and self-confidence faster and more effectively than yelling, sarcasm, or any other harmful method.
You follow your classroom management plan. You let accountability and your undying belief in them do their good work.
